note: Raw-byte stores, materialized identically for both implementations. Chosen to hit the places two languages disagree rather than the places they agree: HTML-escaping defaults, non-ASCII ordering, empty files, nesting, and paths whose order differs between byte and UTF-16 code-unit comparison. A corpus of well-behaved ASCII stores would pass on day one and prove nothing.
not_covered: Symlinks, unreadable files and duplicate paths are specified in WRT-004 §3.1 but are not here: they are filesystem states, not byte content, and a JSON fixture cannot carry them. They need a separate materializing test, and the omission is listed so it is visible rather than assumed away.

plain.note: the ordinary case, so a failure elsewhere is not blamed on complexity

html-escapes.note: Go's encoding/json escapes < > & by default; Python's ensure_ascii=False does not. A path carrying all three is the cheapest way to catch a JCS divergence that would otherwise surface only on someone's real store.

non-ascii.note: UTF-8 preserves code-point order, so byte-sort and code-point-sort must agree. An implementation sorting by UTF-16 code units reorders the astral character against the BMP one.

empty-and-nested.note: an empty file still has a digest, and a nested path is `other`, not skipped

record-shaped-but-not-json.note: role comes from layout, not from parseability -- an unreadable record is exactly the case where naming the bytes matters
